tool.name: Docker
tool.tagline: Build, ship and run applications in portable containers
tool.description: Docker packages an application and everything it needs into an image that runs the same way on a laptop, a CI runner or a production server. It is the standard way to build and run containers, and the foundation for Compose-based development environments and Kubernetes deployments.

concepts.name: Containers vs virtual machines
concepts.summary: A container is an isolated process sharing the host kernel; a VM runs a whole guest OS on virtual hardware.
concepts.why: Knowing what a container really is sets correct expectations about speed, isolation and portability.
concepts.body:
A **virtual machine** emulates hardware. A hypervisor runs several complete guest operating systems, each with its own kernel, drivers and init system. VMs are strongly isolated, but each one costs gigabytes of disk, a slice of reserved RAM and tens of seconds to boot.

A **container** is just a normal process (or a few) on the host, started with kernel features that make it *look* like it has its own machine: its own filesystem, process list, network interfaces and hostname, plus limits on CPU and memory. There is **no guest kernel**; every container shares the host's Linux kernel. So containers start in milliseconds, add almost no memory overhead, and you can run hundreds on one machine.

What a container gives you in practice:

- **Packaging**: the app and its exact dependencies (runtime, libraries, config) travel together as an image, so "works on my machine" becomes "works on every machine with Docker".
- **Isolation**: apps with conflicting dependencies run side by side.
- **Disposability**: containers are cheap to create and destroy, which encourages immutable, reproducible deployments.

The trade-offs follow from the shared kernel. Linux containers need a Linux kernel, so Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows quietly runs a small Linux VM to host them. Isolation is weaker than a VM's: a kernel vulnerability can affect every container on the host, which is why multi-tenant platforms sometimes put containers inside lightweight VMs.

Containers and VMs aren't rivals. In the cloud, your containers usually run inside VMs.
takeaways: Containers are isolated processes sharing the host kernel
VMs virtualize hardware and run a full guest OS
Containers start in milliseconds with little overhead, but isolate less strongly
Docker Desktop runs Linux containers inside a hidden Linux VM
pitfalls: Treating a container like a mini-VM to SSH into and patch by hand — rebuild the image instead.

quiz.q: Why can a container start in milliseconds while a VM takes much longer?
options: A container is a process on the already-running host kernel; no OS has to boot
Containers are compiled ahead of time
VMs must download their image on every start
quiz.explain: No kernel or init system boots; Docker just starts an isolated process.

quiz.q: How do Linux containers run on a Mac with Docker Desktop?
options: Docker translates Linux syscalls to macOS
Inside a lightweight Linux VM that Docker Desktop manages
They can't; only macOS containers run
quiz.explain: Containers need a Linux kernel, so Docker Desktop provides one in a small VM.

concepts.name: Install Docker and run hello-world
concepts.summary: Install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine, verify it with docker version and run your first container.
concepts.why: You need a working client and daemon before anything else, and knowing which is which helps debugging.
concepts.body:
Docker has two parts: the **`docker` CLI** you type commands into, and the **Docker daemon** (`dockerd`) that actually builds images and runs containers. The CLI talks to the daemon over an API, by default through the Unix socket `/var/run/docker.sock`.

How to install:

- **macOS and Windows**: Docker Desktop, which bundles the CLI, a Linux VM running the daemon, Compose, BuildKit and a GUI. On Windows it uses WSL 2.
- **Linux servers**: Docker Engine from Docker's own apt/dnf repository (the distribution's packages are often old), following the install page for your distribution. Docker Desktop for Linux also exists.

Check the installation with `docker version`. It prints a **Client** and a **Server** section; if the server part errors with "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon", the CLI works but the daemon isn't running or you lack permission to its socket. `docker info` shows details such as storage driver, number of containers and images.

Then run the classic test, `docker run hello-world`. Docker looks for the `hello-world` image locally, pulls it from Docker Hub, creates a container from it, runs it (it prints a message and exits), and you're done.

On Linux, Docker commands need root by default. Adding yourself to the `docker` group (`sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, then log in again) removes the `sudo`, but understand what that means: **access to the Docker socket is equivalent to root on the host**, because you can start a container that mounts `/`. Rootless mode, covered later, avoids this.
concepts.code:
docker version
# Client: Version: 29.x ...
# Server: Docker Engine - Community  Version: 29.x ...

docker run hello-world
# Unable to find image 'hello-world:latest' locally
# latest: Pulling from library/hello-world
# Hello from Docker!

docker info --format '{{.ServerVersion}} {{.Driver}}'

# Linux: run docker without sudo (grants root-equivalent access!)
sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER" && newgrp docker
takeaways: The docker CLI is a client; dockerd does the work behind an API socket
docker version shows both; a missing Server section means no daemon access
Membership of the docker group is root-equivalent
pitfalls: Installing the distribution's old docker.io package and then missing current features like BuildKit defaults or Compose v2.

quiz.q: docker version prints the Client section, then 'Cannot connect to the Docker daemon'. What's wrong?
options: The daemon isn't running or you can't access its socket
quiz.explain: The client works; it just can't reach dockerd.

quiz.q: Why is adding a user to the docker group a security decision?
options: Controlling the daemon lets you run containers that mount the host's root filesystem
It shares your Docker Hub password
It makes containers run without isolation
quiz.explain: The daemon runs as root, so whoever controls it effectively has root.

concepts.name: Images and containers
concepts.summary: An image is a read-only template of layers; a container is a running instance of it with its own writable layer.
concepts.why: Every Docker command acts on either images or containers, so keeping them apart avoids most beginner confusion.
concepts.body:
An **image** is a packaged filesystem plus metadata: everything the application needs (a minimal OS userland, runtime, libraries, your code) and settings such as the default command, environment variables and working directory. Images are **read-only** and built from stacked **layers**.

A **container** is a running (or stopped) instance of an image. Docker adds a thin **writable layer** on top of the image's layers, gives the process its isolated environment and starts the default command. You can start many containers from one image; they share the image's read-only layers and each gets its own writable layer. Delete a container and its writable layer, with any files written into it, is gone. The image is untouched.

The class/object analogy works well: the image is the class, containers are instances.

Images are named `registry/namespace/repository:tag`:

- `nginx:1.27` is shorthand for `docker.io/library/nginx:1.27` (Docker Hub, official image).
- `ghcr.io/acme/api:2.3.1` is on GitHub's registry.
- If you omit the tag you get `:latest`, which is just a default tag name, not "the newest version".

Tags are movable labels. The immutable identity of an image is its **digest**, such as `nginx@sha256:4f1c...`, a hash of its content. Production deployments often pin digests for exact reproducibility.

`docker pull` downloads an image; `docker run` pulls automatically if needed. Images are fetched layer by layer, and layers you already have are skipped.
concepts.code:
docker pull nginx:1.27                 # download an image
docker image ls nginx
# REPOSITORY  TAG   IMAGE ID      CREATED      SIZE
# nginx       1.27  9bea9f2796e2  2 weeks ago  192MB

docker run -d --name web1 nginx:1.27   # two containers,
docker run -d --name web2 nginx:1.27   # one image
docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Image}}'
# web2 nginx:1.27
# web1 nginx:1.27

docker image inspect nginx:1.27 --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
# nginx@sha256:...
takeaways: Image = read-only layered template; container = instance + writable layer
Many containers can share one image
Name format: registry/namespace/repo:tag; :latest is only a default tag
Digests are immutable; tags can move
pitfalls: Assuming :latest means the newest release — it's whatever was last pushed with that tag, or nothing at all.

quiz.q: You write files inside a container, then remove the container. What happens to the files?
options: They are saved into the image
They are lost with the container's writable layer
They move to the next container started from the image
They are pushed to the registry
quiz.explain: Container writes go to its own writable layer, deleted with the container (use volumes to persist).

quiz.q: What does docker run postgres refer to, if you have no other context?
options: The newest postgres version ever published
postgres from your OS package manager
quiz.explain: Docker Hub, the library namespace and the latest tag are the defaults.

concepts.name: Running containers with docker run
concepts.summary: Start containers in the foreground or background, name them, give them a terminal and override their command.
concepts.why: docker run is the command you'll use most, and its flags decide how the container behaves.
concepts.body:
`docker run [options] IMAGE [COMMAND] [ARGS]` creates a new container from an image and starts it. The most important options:

- `-d` (detached): run in the background and print the container ID. Without it, the container is attached to your terminal and Ctrl+C stops it.
- `--name api`: give it a memorable name instead of a random one like `quirky_turing`. Names must be unique.
- `-it`: `-i` keeps stdin open and `-t` allocates a terminal. Use both for interactive shells: `docker run -it ubuntu bash`.
- `--rm`: delete the container automatically when it exits. Great for one-off commands.
- `-e KEY=value`: set an environment variable. `-p` publishes ports and `-v` mounts storage; both are covered later.

Anything after the image name **replaces the image's default command** (its `CMD`). `docker run python:3.13 python -c "print(42)"` runs that instead of the default REPL.

The rule that surprises everyone: **a container lives exactly as long as its main process**. The command you run is PID 1 inside the container; when it exits, the container stops. That's why `docker run -d ubuntu` exits immediately: the default command is `bash`, which ends at once with no terminal attached. A container is not a server you keep booted; it is one process.

Every `docker run` makes a **new** container. To restart an existing stopped one, use `docker start`. Using `--rm` for experiments keeps old containers from piling up.
concepts.code:
docker run --rm alpine echo "hello"       # hello (container removed after)
docker run -it --rm ubuntu:24.04 bash     # interactive shell; exit to leave
docker run -d --name cache redis:7        # background service
docker run --rm -e NAME=Ada python:3.13 \
  python -c "import os; print('hi', os.environ['NAME'])"   # hi Ada

docker run -d ubuntu:24.04                # exits at once: bash has no tty
docker ps -a --format '{{.Image}} {{.Status}}'
# ubuntu:24.04  Exited (0) 2 seconds ago
# redis:7       Up 10 seconds
takeaways: -d background, --name, -it interactive, --rm auto-cleanup
Arguments after the image replace its default CMD
The container stops when its main process (PID 1) exits
docker run always creates a new container; docker start reuses one
pitfalls: Putting options after the image name — docker run alpine --rm passes --rm to the container's command, not to Docker.

quiz.q: You run docker run -d ubuntu and it exits immediately. Why?
options: Ubuntu images need a license key
The default command, bash, exits right away without a terminal, so the container stops
quiz.explain: A container lives only as long as its main process.

quiz.q: What does docker run nginx:1.27 echo hi do?
options: Starts nginx and also prints hi
Prints hi instead of starting nginx
quiz.explain: Trailing arguments replace the image's default command.

concepts.name: Managing containers: ps, logs, exec, stop
concepts.summary: List containers, read their logs, open a shell inside them, and stop, restart or remove them.
concepts.why: Day-to-day work with containers is mostly these commands.
concepts.body:
Once containers are running you need to see and control them.

- `docker ps` lists running containers; `docker ps -a` includes stopped ones. Each has an ID (any unique prefix works) and a name.
- `docker logs api` prints what the main process wrote to **stdout and stderr**. `-f` follows, `--tail 100` limits, `--since 10m` filters by time. This is why containerized apps should log to stdout rather than to files.
- `docker exec -it api sh` runs an **additional** process in a running container, here a shell, so you can poke around. Use `bash` if the image has it. `exec` only works while the container is running.
- `docker stop api` sends `SIGTERM` to the main process, waits (10 seconds by default, `-t` to change), then sends `SIGKILL`. Apps should handle SIGTERM to shut down gracefully.
- `docker kill api` sends `SIGKILL` immediately.
- `docker start api` / `docker restart api` start a stopped container again, keeping its writable layer.
- `docker rm api` deletes a stopped container; `docker rm -f api` stops and deletes it.
- `docker inspect api` dumps full JSON details: state, exit code, IP address, mounts, env. Use `--format` to pick fields.
- `docker stats` shows live CPU and memory per container.

Containers that stop keep existing until removed, so `docker ps -a` grows over time. `docker container prune` removes all stopped containers in one go.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name api -p 8000:8000 python:3.13 python -m http.server
docker ps                         # running containers
docker logs -f --tail 20 api      # follow output (Ctrl+C stops following)
docker exec -it api bash          # shell inside; exit to leave
docker exec api ls /              # one-off command
docker inspect api --format '{{.State.Status}} {{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}'
docker stop api                   # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 s
docker ps -a --filter name=api    # Exited (...)
docker start api && docker restart api
docker rm -f api
docker container prune            # remove all stopped containers
takeaways: ps lists; logs shows stdout/stderr; exec runs extra processes inside
stop = SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period
Stopped containers persist until docker rm or prune
inspect --format pulls any detail out of the JSON
pitfalls: Expecting docker logs to show files the app writes to /var/log — it only captures stdout and stderr.

quiz.q: What does docker stop do first?
options: Sends SIGTERM and waits for a grace period
quiz.explain: SIGTERM allows graceful shutdown; SIGKILL follows only if the process doesn't exit in time.

quiz.q: Which command opens a shell inside an already running container named db?
quiz.explain: exec runs a new process in an existing container; run would create a new container.

concepts.name: Managing images and disk space
concepts.summary: List, tag and remove images, and reclaim disk space with docker system df and prune.
concepts.why: Images and build cache quietly eat tens of gigabytes; knowing how to clean up keeps machines healthy.
concepts.body:
Every image you pull or build stays on disk until you remove it, and so do stopped containers, unused volumes and the build cache.

Inspecting images:

- `docker image ls` (or `docker images`): repository, tag, ID, size.
- `docker image ls --filter dangling=true`: **dangling** images, untagged leftovers (`<none>:<none>`) from rebuilding a tag.
- `docker image history nginx:1.27`: the layers and the instructions that created them.
- `docker tag nginx:1.27 myreg.example.com/nginx:prod`: add another name. A tag is just a label; no data is copied.

Removing:

- `docker rmi nginx:1.27` (`docker image rm`) removes a tag, and the image data once no tags or containers reference it. An image used by a container, even a stopped one, can't be removed without `-f`.
- `docker image prune` removes dangling images; `-a` removes every image not used by a container.

The big picture: `docker system df` shows space used by images, containers, local volumes and build cache, and how much is reclaimable. `docker system prune` removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and build cache. Add `-a` for all unused images, and `--volumes` to include unused volumes. Be careful with that last one: volumes hold data such as your local database.

`docker builder prune` clears just the build cache, often the largest item on a developer machine.
concepts.code:
docker image ls
docker image history --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' python:3.13-slim | head -5
docker tag myapp:dev myapp:1.0.0       # second name, same image ID

docker system df
# TYPE           TOTAL  ACTIVE  SIZE     RECLAIMABLE
# Images         41     6       18.2GB   15.9GB (87%)
# Build Cache    312    0       9.4GB    9.4GB

docker image prune                     # dangling images only
docker builder prune --filter until=168h   # build cache older than a week
docker system prune -a                 # everything unused (not volumes)
takeaways: Tags are labels; one image can have many
Dangling images are untagged leftovers from rebuilds
docker system df shows where space goes; prune reclaims it
Only prune volumes deliberately: they hold data
pitfalls: Running docker system prune -a --volumes on a dev box and wiping your local databases.

quiz.q: You rebuilt myapp:dev several times and now see several <none> images. What are they?
options: Dangling images whose tag moved to the newer build
quiz.explain: The tag moved to the new image, leaving the old ones untagged.

concepts.name: Dockerfile basics
concepts.summary: Write a Dockerfile with FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE and CMD to package your own app.
concepts.why: A Dockerfile is the recipe for your image; every containerized project has one.
concepts.body:
A **Dockerfile** is a text file of instructions that build an image, executed top to bottom:

- `FROM python:3.13-slim`: the base image to start from. Always first.
- `WORKDIR /app`: set (and create) the working directory for later instructions and for the container.
- `COPY requirements.txt .`: copy files from the **build context** (your project folder) into the image. `ADD` can also fetch URLs and unpack archives; prefer `COPY` unless you need that.
- `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt`: run a command at **build time** and save the result in the image.
- `ENV PORT=8000`: an environment variable available at build time and at run time.
- `EXPOSE 8000`: documents the port the app listens on. It doesn't publish anything by itself.
- `USER app`: run later steps and the container as this user.
- `CMD ["python", "app.py"]`: the default command when a container starts. There can be one CMD; a later one wins.

`RUN` happens once, during the build; `CMD` happens every time a container starts. Mixing them up is the classic beginner bug.

Use the **exec form** with a JSON array (`CMD ["python", "app.py"]`) rather than the shell form (`CMD python app.py`). The shell form runs your app under `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell is PID 1 and `docker stop`'s SIGTERM never reaches your app.

`ENTRYPOINT` sets a fixed executable, and `CMD` then supplies default arguments: with `ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"]` and `CMD ["app:app"]`, `docker run img other:app` swaps just the argument. Use it when the image is essentially one command.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
ENV PORT=8000
EXPOSE 8000
RUN useradd --create-home app
USER app
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
takeaways: RUN executes at build time; CMD is the default at container start
Use exec form ["cmd", "arg"] so your app is PID 1 and gets signals
EXPOSE only documents a port; publishing happens at docker run
ENTRYPOINT fixes the executable; CMD gives default arguments
pitfalls: Writing RUN python app.py to 'start' the app — that runs during the build and blocks or bakes nothing useful.

quiz.q: When does a RUN instruction execute?
options: Once, while the image is being built
Only when you run docker exec
quiz.explain: RUN results are stored in an image layer; CMD is what runs at container start.

quiz.q: Why prefer CMD ["node", "server.js"] over CMD node server.js?
options: The shell form is not allowed in modern Docker
Exec form makes the image smaller
Exec form runs node as PID 1, so it receives SIGTERM from docker stop
Shell form can't read environment variables
quiz.explain: Shell form wraps the command in /bin/sh -c, which typically doesn't forward signals.

concepts.name: Building and tagging images
concepts.summary: Turn a Dockerfile into an image with docker build, understand the build context, and tag versions properly.
concepts.why: Building and naming images well is the bridge between your code and anything you deploy.
concepts.body:
`docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` builds an image from the `Dockerfile` in the current directory and tags it `myapp:1.0`.

The final `.` is the **build context**: the set of files the builder may access. `COPY` paths are relative to it, and nothing outside it can be copied (`COPY ../secret .` fails). With modern Docker the build runs in **BuildKit**, which transfers only the files the build actually uses, but large contexts still slow builds; that's what `.dockerignore` is for.

Useful options:

- `-f docker/Dockerfile.prod`: use a Dockerfile elsewhere or with another name.
- `-t` can be repeated: `-t myapp:1.4.2 -t myapp:1.4 -t myapp:latest`.
- `--build-arg VERSION=1.4.2`: pass a value to an `ARG` instruction.
- `--no-cache`: rebuild every step from scratch.
- `--progress=plain`: full, unabridged output, handy when debugging a failing `RUN`.

**Tagging strategy** matters once images leave your laptop. Tag every build with something immutable and traceable, such as a semantic version (`1.4.2`) or the git commit (`git-3f9a2c1`), and optionally move convenience tags (`1.4`, `latest`) along. Deploy the immutable tag, so you always know exactly what's running and can roll back.

`docker tag` adds names after the fact: `docker tag myapp:1.4.2 registry.example.com/team/myapp:1.4.2` prepares an image for pushing to a registry. Run the result with `docker run myapp:1.4.2`.
concepts.code:
docker build -t myapp:dev .
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.prod \
  --build-arg VERSION=1.4.2 \
  -t myapp:1.4.2 -t myapp:git-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) .

docker image ls myapp
# myapp  1.4.2        5e1c0a7b9d2f  ...
# myapp  git-3f9a2c1  5e1c0a7b9d2f  ...   <- same image ID
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 myapp:1.4.2
docker build --no-cache --progress=plain -t myapp:debug .
takeaways: The trailing . is the build context; COPY can't reach outside it
-t can be given several times; tags are just names for one image ID
Deploy immutable tags (version or commit), not latest
pitfalls: Running docker build from your home directory with . as context, making Docker scan thousands of unrelated files.

quiz.q: Your Dockerfile has COPY ../shared/lib ./lib. What happens with docker build . in the project folder?
options: It fails because the path is outside the build context
It follows the path only with --no-cache
quiz.explain: The builder only sees files inside the context directory.

concepts.name: Layers and the build cache
concepts.summary: Each Dockerfile instruction makes a cached layer; order instructions so dependency installs are reused across builds.
concepts.why: A well-ordered Dockerfile rebuilds in seconds instead of minutes, all day long.
concepts.body:
Each instruction that changes the filesystem (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`) produces a **layer**: a diff of files added, changed or deleted. The image is the stack of these layers. Metadata instructions like `ENV` and `CMD` only change the image config.

When you rebuild, the builder checks each step against its **cache**. A step is reused if its instruction is unchanged *and*, for `COPY`/`ADD`, the checksums of the copied files are unchanged. The crucial rule: **once a step misses the cache, every step after it is rebuilt.**

So order instructions from least to most frequently changing. The standard pattern copies the dependency manifest first, installs, and only then copies the source:

```dockerfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```

Editing source code now invalidates only the last `COPY`; the slow `npm ci` stays cached until the lockfile changes. Copying everything first would reinstall dependencies on every code change.

Other layer facts that matter:

- Deleting a file in a later layer **does not shrink the image**; the earlier layer still contains it. Clean up in the same `RUN` that created the mess: `apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`.
- `RUN apt-get update` alone in its own step gets cached forever, leading to stale package lists; always chain it with the install.
- The cache key is the instruction text, not the outside world, so `RUN curl .../latest.tar.gz` won't refetch. Use `--no-cache` or a changing build arg when you need fresh content.

`docker image history <image>` shows each layer's size and the instruction that made it.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app

# 1. Rarely changes: cached unless the lockfile changes
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# 2. Changes on every commit: only this layer and below rebuild
COPY . .

# Install + clean up in ONE layer, or the cleanup saves nothing
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
takeaways: Each RUN/COPY/ADD creates a layer; a cache miss rebuilds everything after it
Copy dependency manifests and install before copying source
Clean up in the same RUN; later deletions don't shrink earlier layers
Chain apt-get update with install in one RUN
pitfalls: COPY . . near the top of the Dockerfile, so every code edit reinstalls all dependencies.

quiz.q: You change one line in src/app.js. Which steps rebuild in the example Dockerfile?
options: COPY . . and every step after it
quiz.explain: The COPY . . step's file checksums changed, so it and everything after it miss the cache.

quiz.q: A RUN step downloads a 300 MB archive and a later RUN deletes it. How much does the deletion save in the final image?
options: Nothing; the earlier layer still contains the file
It depends on the base image
quiz.explain: Layers are additive; the deletion is recorded as a whiteout in a new layer.

concepts.name: Keeping the build context lean: .dockerignore
concepts.summary: List files to exclude from the build context in .dockerignore to speed up builds, improve caching and avoid leaking secrets.
concepts.why: Without it, node_modules, .git and .env files end up slowing builds or, worse, inside your image.
concepts.body:
The build context is everything in the directory you pass to `docker build`. A **`.dockerignore`** file in the root of the context lists patterns to exclude, much like `.gitignore`.

Why it matters:

- **Speed**: sending a 2 GB `node_modules` or `.git` directory to the builder wastes time on every build.
- **Cache stability**: `COPY . .` checksums everything it copies. If `.git` or log files are included, the cache breaks whenever they change, even when your code didn't.
- **Security**: `.env` files, SSH keys and cloud credentials sitting in the project folder get baked into the image by `COPY . .`, and anyone who pulls the image can read them.
- **Correctness**: copying your host's `node_modules` (built for macOS) over the container's Linux-built ones causes confusing native-module errors.

Syntax essentials:

- One pattern per line; `#` starts a comment.
- Paths are relative to the context root; `*` matches within a path segment, `**` across any number of directories.
- `!pattern` re-includes something excluded earlier, and the last matching line wins.
- Some teams invert it: start with `*`, then allow only what's needed with `!src` and `!package*.json`.

The file must sit at the **root of the build context**, not necessarily next to the Dockerfile. With BuildKit you can also give a Dockerfile its own ignore file by naming it after it, for example `Dockerfile.prod.dockerignore`.
concepts.code:
# .dockerignore
.git
.gitignore
**/node_modules
**/__pycache__
*.log
dist/
coverage/

# secrets and local config
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
**/*.pem

# not needed inside the image
Dockerfile*
compose*.yaml
README.md
takeaways: .dockerignore excludes files from the build context
It speeds up builds, stabilises the cache and keeps secrets out
It must be at the context root; ! re-includes; last match wins
pitfalls: Relying on .gitignore — Docker ignores it; only .dockerignore affects the build context.

quiz.q: Your build cache keeps busting on COPY . . even though source files didn't change. What is a likely cause?
options: The base image is too old
Files like .git or logs are in the context and change on every commit
quiz.explain: COPY checksums everything copied, so churny files invalidate it unless ignored.

concepts.name: Multi-stage builds
concepts.summary: Use several FROM stages to compile with full toolchains and ship only the result in a small final image.
concepts.why: It's the single most effective way to make production images small and secure.
concepts.body:
Building software needs compilers, dev headers, test tools and package caches; running it needs none of that. A **multi-stage build** puts several `FROM` instructions in one Dockerfile. Each starts a new stage, and you copy just the artifacts you want from earlier stages with `COPY --from=<stage>`. Only the **last stage** becomes the image (unless you pick another), so build tools never reach production.

Typical shapes:

- **Compiled languages** (Go, Rust): build in `golang:1.25`, copy the single binary into `gcr.io/distroless/static` or even `scratch`. The image drops from about 1 GB to about 10 MB.
- **Frontend apps**: `npm run build` in a Node stage, copy the `dist/` folder into an `nginx` stage.
- **Interpreted apps**: install dependencies with build tools present (to compile native wheels), then copy the installed packages or virtualenv into a slim runtime stage.

Name stages with `AS`, as in `FROM golang:1.25 AS build`, and reference them by name.

Other useful tricks:

- `docker build --target test .` stops at a given stage, so one Dockerfile can define dev, test and prod images.
- `COPY --from=nginx:1.27 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf .` copies from any image, not just stages.
- BuildKit builds independent stages **in parallel** and skips stages the target doesn't depend on.

Make sure the runtime stage really has what the program needs at run time: CA certificates, timezone data, the C library if the binary is dynamically linked (static Go binaries need `CGO_ENABLED=0`).
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.25 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server ./cmd/server

FROM build AS test
RUN go test ./...

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 AS prod
COPY --from=build /out/server /server
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

# docker build -t api:prod .              -> last stage (prod), ~10 MB
# docker build --target test -t api:test .
takeaways: Only the final (or --target) stage becomes the image
COPY --from=stage copies artifacts between stages
--target lets one Dockerfile produce dev, test and prod images
Check the runtime stage has certs, libc and data files the app needs
pitfalls: Shipping a dynamically linked binary into scratch or distroless/static, where it fails with a confusing 'no such file or directory'.

quiz.q: In a multi-stage Dockerfile without --target, which stage becomes the image?
quiz.explain: The final stage is the default target; earlier stages exist only to feed it.

quiz.q: What does COPY --from=build /out/app /app do?
options: Copies /out/app from the stage named build into the current stage
quiz.explain: --from takes files from an earlier stage (or any image) instead of the build context.

concepts.name: Persisting data with volumes
concepts.summary: Store data outside a container's writable layer in Docker-managed named volumes that survive container removal.
concepts.why: Databases and uploads must outlive containers, which are meant to be disposable.
concepts.body:
A container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed, and writing heavily to it is slow. For data that must persist, such as a database's files, use a **volume**: storage managed by Docker, living outside any container, mounted at a path inside it.

```bash
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17
```

Remove and recreate the `db` container (to upgrade the image, say) with the same `-v pgdata:...` and the data is still there.

The more explicit `--mount` syntax says the same thing and is easier to read in scripts: `--mount type=volume,src=pgdata,dst=/var/lib/postgresql/data`.

Things to know:

- If you mount a volume that doesn't exist, Docker creates it.
- When an **empty** volume is mounted over a directory that has content in the image, Docker copies that content into the volume first. Handy for seeding config.
- `-v /data` with no name creates an **anonymous** volume with a random ID. They're removed along with the container if you used `--rm` (or `docker rm -v`); otherwise they linger.
- Volumes can be shared by several containers at once; append `:ro` to mount read-only.
- `docker volume ls`, `inspect`, `rm` and `prune` manage them. Removing containers never removes named volumes, which is good for data and bad for disk space.

To back up a volume, mount it into a throwaway container together with a host folder and tar it up. That works the same everywhere, including Docker Desktop, where volume files live inside the VM rather than on your Mac or PC.
concepts.code:
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev \
  --mount type=volume,src=pgdata,dst=/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17

docker rm -f db                  # container gone...
docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17   # ...data still there

# Back up the volume to ./pgdata.tgz
docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data:ro -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data .

docker volume ls
docker volume inspect pgdata --format '{{.Mountpoint}}'
takeaways: Volumes are Docker-managed storage that outlives containers
-v name:/path or --mount type=volume,src=...,dst=...
Empty volumes are pre-filled from the image's content at that path
Back up with a throwaway container that tars the volume
pitfalls: Running a database without a volume, then losing all data on docker rm.

quiz.q: You run docker rm -f db on a container using named volume pgdata. What happens to pgdata?
options: It is deleted with the container
It is kept until you remove it explicitly
It is converted to an image layer
quiz.explain: Named volumes have their own lifecycle independent of containers.

quiz.q: An empty new volume is mounted at /etc/app, where the image has default config files. What does the container see?
options: The image's files, copied into the volume first
A merged view that isn't saved
quiz.explain: Docker populates an empty named volume with the image's content at the mount point.

concepts.name: Bind mounts and tmpfs
concepts.summary: Mount a host directory into a container for live development, or an in-memory tmpfs for scratch data.
concepts.why: Bind mounts give the edit-and-reload loop for development; knowing their pitfalls saves hours.
concepts.body:
A **bind mount** maps an existing path on the host directly into the container. Unlike a volume, Docker doesn't manage it; the container sees your real files, and changes go both ways instantly.

```bash
docker run -v "$PWD":/app -w /app node:22 npm run dev
```

That is the classic development setup: your editor changes files on the host, the dev server in the container reloads. The `--mount` form is `--mount type=bind,src="$PWD",dst=/app`; unlike `-v`, it errors if the source path doesn't exist instead of creating an empty directory, which catches typos.

Key behaviours and gotchas:

- A bind mount **hides** whatever the image had at that path. Mounting your project over `/app` also hides the `node_modules` installed in the image. A common fix is an extra anonymous volume for that subfolder: `-v /app/node_modules`.
- **Permissions**: files are owned by numeric UIDs. A container running as root creates root-owned files in your project; a non-root container may be unable to write host files. Run with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` on Linux when needed.
- **Performance** on Docker Desktop is lower than on native Linux, because files cross the VM boundary; synchronized file shares or volumes help for heavy I/O.
- Append `:ro` (or `readonly` with `--mount`) for config files the container should only read.
- Bind mounts tie a container to the host's directory layout, so use them for development and for specific host files, and use volumes for application data.

A **tmpfs** mount (`--tmpfs /tmp`) lives only in memory and vanishes when the container stops. Use it for scratch files and secrets that must never touch disk, and pair it with `--read-only` root filesystems.
concepts.code:
# Live-reload dev server, keeping the image's node_modules
docker run --rm -it -p 5173:5173 \
  -v "$PWD":/app -v /app/node_modules -w /app \
  node:22 npm run dev -- --host

# Read-only config file from the host
docker run -d --name proxy \
  --mount type=bind,src="$PWD"/nginx.conf,dst=/etc/nginx/nginx.conf,readonly \
  -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27

# Avoid root-owned files in your project (Linux)
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" alpine touch out.txt

# In-memory scratch space on a read-only container
docker run --rm --read-only --tmpfs /tmp alpine sh -c 'echo hi > /tmp/x && cat /tmp/x'
takeaways: Bind mounts expose a host path directly; changes are live both ways
They hide the image's content at the mount point
Watch UID ownership and Docker Desktop I/O performance
tmpfs mounts are in-memory and disappear on stop
pitfalls: Mounting the project over /app and wondering where node_modules went.

quiz.q: You bind-mount your project to /app, but the image installed dependencies in /app/node_modules. What does the container see?
options: Your host's /app contents only; the image's node_modules is hidden
quiz.explain: A mount replaces the view of the directory underneath it.

quiz.q: Which mount type should hold a production database's data?
options: A bind mount to the project folder
quiz.explain: Volumes are managed by Docker, portable across hosts and suited to persistent app data.

concepts.name: Publishing ports
concepts.summary: Make a container's service reachable from the host with -p host:container, and bind it to the right interface.
concepts.why: Nothing inside a container is reachable from your browser until you publish its port.
concepts.body:
Containers get their own network namespace with a private IP. A server listening on port 80 inside a container is not reachable from the host or the outside world until you **publish** the port:

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
```

The format is `-p [host_ip:]host_port:container_port[/protocol]`. Here, host port 8080 forwards to container port 80, so `http://localhost:8080` reaches nginx.

Details that matter:

- By default the port is bound on **all host interfaces** (`0.0.0.0` and `::`), so it's reachable from your network, not just localhost. On Linux, Docker's own iptables/nftables rules mean it can bypass host firewalls such as ufw. For anything local-only, use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80`.
- Two containers can't publish the same host port. Pick different host ports (`8081:80`, `8082:80`) or put a reverse proxy in front.
- `-p 80` (no host port) picks a random free host port; `docker port web` shows the mapping.
- `-P` publishes every port the image `EXPOSE`s to random host ports. `EXPOSE` alone publishes nothing.
- UDP needs `/udp`: `-p 5353:53/udp`.

The app inside must listen on `0.0.0.0`, not `127.0.0.1`. A dev server bound to the container's own loopback is unreachable through a published port. Many frameworks default to localhost, so this is the number one "port is published but connection refused" cause.

Containers talking to each other don't need published ports at all; they use a shared network, covered next.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
curl -s localhost:8080 | head -1          # <!DOCTYPE html>

docker run -d --name admin -p 127.0.0.1:9000:80 nginx:1.27   # local only
docker run -d --name rand -p 80 nginx:1.27
docker port rand                          # 80/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:49154

# App must listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 python:3.13 \
  python -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0
takeaways: -p host:container publishes a port; EXPOSE is documentation only
Default binding is all interfaces; use 127.0.0.1: for local-only
The app must listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container
Container-to-container traffic doesn't need published ports
pitfalls: Publishing a database with -p 5432:5432 on a cloud VM and exposing it to the internet despite the firewall.

quiz.q: The port is published with -p 3000:3000 but the browser gets 'connection refused'. The app logs 'listening on 127.0.0.1:3000'. Fix?
quiz.explain: Traffic arrives on the container's network interface, not its loopback.

quiz.q: What does EXPOSE 8080 in a Dockerfile do by itself?
options: Documents the port and lets -P publish it
quiz.explain: EXPOSE is metadata; publishing requires -p or -P at run time.

concepts.name: Container networking
concepts.summary: Connect containers on user-defined bridge networks so they reach each other by name via Docker's built-in DNS.
concepts.why: Multi-container apps (app + database + cache) depend on containers finding each other reliably.
concepts.body:
Docker gives containers networking through **network drivers**:

- **bridge**: a private virtual network on one host. The default for containers.
- **host**: the container uses the host's network stack directly, with no isolation and no port mapping. Linux only, and occasionally used for performance.
- **none**: no networking at all.
- **overlay** (Swarm) and **macvlan/ipvlan** cover multi-host and LAN-attached setups.

Containers started without `--network` join the **default bridge**, where they can reach each other only by IP address. Don't use it for apps. Create a **user-defined bridge network** instead:

```bash
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapi
```

On a user-defined network, Docker's **embedded DNS** resolves container names (and `--network-alias` names) to their current IPs, so `api` connects to `postgres://db:5432`. IPs change when containers are recreated; names don't. Networks also isolate: containers on different networks can't talk unless one is attached to both (`docker network connect`).

Notice there's no `-p` on the database: container-to-container traffic flows over the network on the container's real port. Publish only what the outside world needs, such as the API or a reverse proxy.

Reaching the host from a container: Docker Desktop provides `host.docker.internal`; on Linux add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway`.

`docker network inspect appnet` lists connected containers and their IPs. Docker Compose creates a network per project automatically, which is why services there can reach each other by service name.
concepts.code:
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet -p 8000:8000 \
  -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:dev@db:5432/postgres myapi:1.0

# Name resolution from inside the network
docker run --rm --network appnet alpine nslookup db
# Name: db  Address: 172.18.0.2

docker network inspect appnet --format '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{end}}'
# db api

# Reach a service running on the host (Linux)
docker run --rm --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway alpine \
  ping -c1 host.docker.internal
takeaways: Use user-defined bridge networks; the default bridge has no name DNS
Containers on the same network reach each other by name on container ports
Only publish ports for traffic from outside Docker
host.docker.internal reaches the host (host-gateway on Linux)
pitfalls: Hard-coding container IP addresses — they change whenever containers are recreated.

quiz.q: api and db are both on user-defined network appnet; db has no -p flag. Can api connect to db:5432?
options: Yes, via Docker's DNS on the shared network
quiz.explain: Containers on the same network talk directly; publishing is only for the host/outside.

quiz.q: Two containers on the default bridge network try to reach each other by name. What happens?
options: It works the same as on user-defined networks
Name resolution fails; the default bridge has no automatic DNS for names
quiz.explain: Automatic name resolution is a feature of user-defined networks.

concepts.name: Environment variables and configuration
concepts.summary: Configure containers at run time with environment variables, env files and mounted config, and know ARG from ENV.
concepts.why: One image should run in dev, staging and production; configuration is what changes between them.
concepts.body:
Build images once and configure them per environment at run time, following the twelve-factor idea that config lives in the environment, not in the image.

Ways to pass configuration:

- `-e LOG_LEVEL=debug`: one variable. `-e API_KEY` with no value passes through the variable from your shell.
- `--env-file prod.env`: many `KEY=value` lines from a file.
- **Config files** via a bind mount or volume, for structured configuration like `nginx.conf`.
- Secrets via files: orchestrators (Compose, Swarm, Kubernetes) mount secrets as files, and many official images accept `*_FILE` variants such as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE`.

In the Dockerfile there are two variable instructions, often confused:

- **`ARG`** exists only **during the build**. Set it with `--build-arg`. Useful for versions: `ARG NODE_VERSION=22` then `FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}`. An `ARG` declared before `FROM` must be redeclared inside the stage to be used there.
- **`ENV`** is set during the build **and** persists into every container as a default, overridable with `-e`.

Neither is a safe place for secrets. Both are recorded in the image (`docker history` and `docker inspect` reveal them), and environment variables of a running container are visible to anyone with access to `docker inspect`. Use BuildKit secret mounts at build time and secret files at run time.

Make your app read its config from the environment with sane defaults, and fail fast with a clear message when a required variable is missing.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile excerpt
#   ARG APP_VERSION=dev          # build time only
#   ENV PORT=8000 LOG_LEVEL=info # defaults for every container
#   LABEL version=$APP_VERSION

docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.4.2 -t api:1.4.2 .

cat > prod.env <<'END'
LOG_LEVEL=warn
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app@db:5432/app
END
docker run -d --env-file prod.env -e PORT=9000 -p 9000:9000 api:1.4.2
docker exec $(docker ps -lq) printenv LOG_LEVEL PORT    # warn / 9000

docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.Env}}' api:1.4.2   # ENV is visible!
takeaways: Build once, configure at run time with -e, --env-file and mounted files
ARG = build time only; ENV = build time and container default
ARG and ENV values are visible in image metadata: never put secrets there
pitfalls: Baking a production API key into the image with ENV — anyone who can pull the image can read it.

quiz.q: Which Dockerfile instruction's value is NOT available to the running container?
quiz.explain: ARG exists only during the build (unless copied into an ENV).

quiz.q: Why shouldn't secrets be passed as build args?
options: Build args are limited to 64 characters
They're recorded in image metadata and history
quiz.explain: Build args used in steps appear in the image history; use BuildKit secret mounts.

concepts.name: Docker Compose
concepts.summary: Define a multi-container app (services, networks, volumes) in compose.yaml and run it with docker compose up.
concepts.why: Compose turns a page of docker run commands into one versioned file that the whole team runs the same way.
concepts.body:
Real apps are several containers: API, database, cache, worker. **Docker Compose** describes them declaratively in `compose.yaml` and manages them as one project with the `docker compose` command (Compose v2, built into the Docker CLI).

The file's top-level keys:

- `services`: each service is a container definition, with `image` or `build`, `ports`, `environment`, `env_file`, `volumes`, `depends_on`, `command` and so on, mirroring `docker run` flags.
- `volumes`: named volumes the services use.
- `networks`: optional; by default Compose creates one network for the project, and every service can reach every other **by service name**.

The old top-level `version:` key is obsolete and ignored.

Core commands, run in the folder with the file:

- `docker compose up -d`: build or pull as needed, create the network and volumes, start everything in the background. Run it again after editing the file and only changed services are recreated.
- `docker compose ps`, `logs -f api`, `exec db psql -U postgres`.
- `docker compose up -d --build`: rebuild images first.
- `docker compose down`: stop and remove containers and the network. Volumes are kept unless you add `-v`.

Compose substitutes variables like `${TAG:-latest}` from your shell or from a `.env` file next to `compose.yaml`. That `.env` is for **interpolating the YAML**; `env_file:` passes variables **into containers**. They are different mechanisms.

`depends_on` controls start **order** only; by default it doesn't wait for the database to be ready. Combine it with healthchecks (`condition: service_healthy`), covered later, or make the app retry its connection.
concepts.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    image: acme/api:${TAG:-dev}
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8000:8000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:dev@db:5432/postgres
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  pgdata:
# docker compose up -d --build ; docker compose logs -f api ; docker compose down
takeaways: compose.yaml declares services, volumes and networks for one project
Services reach each other by service name on the project network
up -d is idempotent; down keeps volumes unless -v
.env interpolates the YAML; env_file passes variables into containers
pitfalls: Assuming depends_on waits until the database accepts connections — it only orders startup unless you use a health condition.

quiz.q: How does the api service connect to the db service in the same compose project?
options: Via the db service name, e.g. db:5432
Only via a published host port
It needs a manual docker network connect
quiz.explain: Compose puts services on a shared project network with DNS for service names.

quiz.q: What does docker compose down do to named volumes by default?
quiz.explain: Volumes survive down; add -v to remove them.

concepts.name: Registries: pushing and pulling images
concepts.summary: Push images to Docker Hub or a private registry, authenticate with docker login, and pin by digest.
concepts.why: Registries are how images move from your build to servers, CI and teammates.
concepts.body:
A **registry** stores and serves images. Docker Hub (`docker.io`) is the default; others include GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`), GitLab's registry, cloud registries (Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure ACR) and self-hosted ones such as Harbor.

The image name says where it goes: `ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2` means registry `ghcr.io`, repository `acme/api`, tag `1.4.2`. To push, the local image must carry that name:

```bash
docker login ghcr.io
docker tag api:1.4.2 ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
```

Pushes and pulls are layer-based: layers the registry already has, such as your base image's layers, aren't uploaded again.

**Authentication**: `docker login` stores credentials in a credential helper (the OS keychain on Desktop) or, failing that, in `~/.docker/config.json`. Use access tokens rather than passwords, and short-lived tokens in CI.

**Tags vs digests**: a tag is mutable; someone can push a different image under `1.4.2` tomorrow. The **digest** (`ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:...`), printed after each push, is the content hash and can never change. Pin digests in production manifests when you need guaranteed reproducibility; tools such as Renovate keep them updated.

**Docker Hub limits**: anonymous and free-account pulls are rate-limited. CI systems that pull a lot should authenticate, use a pull-through cache or mirror, or pull base images from another registry.

Private repositories require `docker login` on every machine that pulls them, including servers and CI runners.
concepts.code:
echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u my-user --password-stdin
docker build -t ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 -t ghcr.io/acme/api:latest .
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
# 1.4.2: digest: sha256:7c3e...a1f9 size: 1784
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:latest       # layers already exist: instant

# Pull an exact, immutable image
docker pull ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:7c3e...a1f9
docker image inspect ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'
docker logout ghcr.io
takeaways: The registry host is part of the image name; tag images to match before pushing
Push/pull transfer only missing layers
Tags can be overwritten; digests are immutable
Authenticate CI to avoid Docker Hub rate limits
pitfalls: Passing a password with -p on the command line, where it lands in shell history — use --password-stdin.

quiz.q: You push api:1.4.2 to a registry, and later a colleague pushes a different build with the same tag. Which reference still gets your original image?
quiz.explain: Digests identify content immutably; tags can be repointed.

concepts.name: Small and secure images
concepts.summary: Shrink and harden images: minimal bases, non-root users, pinned versions, no secrets, vulnerability scanning.
concepts.why: Every package in an image is attack surface and download time; production images should carry only what runs.
concepts.body:
Image size and security improve together: fewer packages means fewer vulnerabilities, smaller downloads and faster scaling.

**Choose a minimal base.** Roughly from largest to smallest:

- Full distro images (`python:3.13`, `node:22`): convenient, hundreds of MB, many packages.
- `-slim` variants: Debian with the extras removed. A good default for interpreted languages.
- `alpine`: tiny, but uses musl libc, which can break or slow down prebuilt binaries and Python wheels. Test before switching.
- **Distroless** (`gcr.io/distroless/...`) and hardened minimal images: only the runtime, no shell or package manager.
- `scratch`: empty, for static binaries.

Combine with multi-stage builds so compilers never reach the final image.

**Don't run as root.** Add a user and switch with `USER 10001` (numeric IDs work everywhere, including with Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot`). Root inside a container is not fully root on the host, but it makes container escapes and mistakes far more damaging.

**Keep secrets out.** Not in `COPY`, `ARG` or `ENV`; use `.dockerignore`, BuildKit secret mounts and runtime secrets. Anything in any layer can be extracted, even if a later layer deletes it.

**Pin and update.** Pin base images to specific versions (or digests) for reproducibility, and rebuild regularly so OS security fixes land. Automate both with Dependabot or Renovate.

**Scan and attest.** `docker scout cves <image>` (or Trivy, Grype) lists known CVEs per package. `docker buildx build --sbom=true --provenance=true` attaches a software bill of materials and build provenance to the image.

At run time, add `--read-only`, `--cap-drop ALL` and `--security-opt no-new-privileges` where the app allows.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim AS build
RUN python -m venv /venv
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN /venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.13-slim
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app
COPY --from=build /venv /venv
COPY --chown=10001:10001 src/ /app/
WORKDIR /app
USER 10001
ENV PATH=/venv/bin:$PATH PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000", "app:app"]

# docker scout cves api:1.4.2
# docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL api:1.4.2
takeaways: Smaller base = fewer CVEs and faster pulls; test alpine's musl before adopting
Run as a numeric non-root USER
Secrets in any layer are recoverable: keep them out of the build
Pin versions, rebuild often, scan with docker scout or Trivy
pitfalls: Switching to alpine for size and then hitting slow or broken musl builds of native Python/Node packages.

quiz.q: Why is a distroless image harder to attack than a full distro image?
options: It contains no shell or package manager and far fewer packages
quiz.explain: Less software means fewer vulnerabilities and fewer tools for an attacker to use.

quiz.q: A Dockerfile COPYs id_rsa, uses it in a RUN, then deletes it in the next RUN. Is the key in the image?
options: Only if the image is pushed
Yes, the earlier layer still contains it
quiz.explain: Layers are immutable; deletion in a later layer doesn't remove the data from earlier ones.

concepts.name: Healthchecks and restart policies
concepts.summary: Tell Docker how to test that your app works with HEALTHCHECK, and how to recover from crashes with restart policies.
concepts.why: A running process isn't necessarily a working service; health and restart settings close that gap.
concepts.body:
Docker only knows whether the main process is running. A web server stuck in a deadlock is still "Up". A **healthcheck** gives Docker a command to test real health:

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/healthz || exit 1
```

Docker runs the command inside the container on that schedule. Exit code 0 means healthy, 1 unhealthy. The status moves from `starting` to `healthy`, or to `unhealthy` after `retries` consecutive failures, and shows in `docker ps` and `docker inspect`. `--start-period` gives slow starters time before failures count. The check needs its tool (curl, wget or a tiny binary) in the image, which matters with distroless images. You can also set or override it at run time (`--health-cmd`) or in Compose (`healthcheck:`).

What uses health status: Compose's `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` waits for it, Swarm replaces unhealthy tasks, and monitoring can alert on it. Plain `docker run` does **not** restart an unhealthy container by itself. (Kubernetes ignores Docker healthchecks and uses its own probes.)

**Restart policies** (`--restart`) handle crashes and reboots:

- `no` (default): never restart.
- `on-failure[:5]`: restart only on a non-zero exit, optionally at most 5 times.
- `always`: restart whenever it stops; a container you stopped manually comes back when the daemon restarts.
- `unless-stopped`: like `always`, but a manual `docker stop` is respected across daemon restarts.

Docker waits progressively longer between restarts of a crash-looping container. For servers, `unless-stopped` with a healthcheck is a sensible single-host baseline.
concepts.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev }
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
# docker compose ps  ->  db  Up 20 seconds (healthy)
takeaways: HEALTHCHECK runs a command in the container: 0 healthy, 1 unhealthy
Plain Docker reports unhealthy but doesn't restart it; Compose and Swarm can act on it
Restart policies: no, on-failure, always, unless-stopped
depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for readiness
pitfalls: Using a healthcheck command (like curl) that isn't installed in the image, so the container is always unhealthy.

quiz.q: A container's healthcheck reports unhealthy and it runs with --restart always. What does Docker do?
options: Keeps it running and reports it as unhealthy
quiz.explain: Restart policies react to the process exiting, not to health status.

quiz.q: Which restart policy keeps a container you stopped manually from coming back after a daemon restart?
quiz.explain: unless-stopped respects a manual stop; always restarts it when the daemon starts.

concepts.name: Resource limits
concepts.summary: Cap a container's memory, CPU and process count, and recognise OOM kills.
concepts.why: Without limits, one leaky container can starve every other service on the host.
concepts.body:
By default a container may use all of the host's CPU and memory. Limits are enforced by the kernel's control groups, and you set them on `docker run` (or in Compose):

- `--memory 512m`: hard memory limit. If the container exceeds it, the kernel's **OOM killer** kills a process in it, usually the main one, and the container exits with code **137**. `docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'` confirms it.
- `--memory-swap`: memory plus swap. Setting it equal to `--memory` disables swap for the container.
- `--memory-reservation`: a soft limit applied when the host is under memory pressure.
- `--cpus 1.5`: at most 1.5 CPUs' worth of time. Exceeding it means **throttling** (slower), not a kill.
- `--cpu-shares`: a relative weight that only matters when CPUs are contended.
- `--cpuset-cpus 0,1`: pin to specific cores.
- `--pids-limit 200`: cap the number of processes, which stops fork bombs.

`docker stats` shows live usage against limits. `docker update --memory 1g api` changes limits on a running container.

Make the **runtime aware** of its limits. Modern JVMs (container support is on by default) and Go read cgroup limits, though Go's `GOMAXPROCS` only became container-aware in recent versions. Node sizes its heap from container memory in recent versions too, but `--max-old-space-size` is still common. Many apps size worker pools from the host's CPU count, so set worker counts explicitly.

In Compose, use `deploy.resources.limits` (`cpus`, `memory`) and optionally `reservations`; `docker compose up` applies them.

Set limits from measurements: watch real usage under load, then add headroom. A limit that's too tight produces mysterious exit 137 restarts.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name api --memory 512m --memory-swap 512m \
  --cpus 1.5 --pids-limit 200 acme/api:1.4.2

docker stats --no-stream api
# NAME  CPU %   MEM USAGE / LIMIT    MEM %   PIDS
# api   37.2%   311MiB / 512MiB      60.7%   23

docker inspect api --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} OOM={{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# 137 OOM=true   (after a memory spike)

docker update --memory 1g --memory-swap 1g api

# compose.yaml equivalent:
#   deploy:
#     resources:
#       limits: { cpus: "1.5", memory: 512M }
takeaways: Default is unlimited; set --memory, --cpus and --pids-limit for production
Memory over the limit = OOM kill (exit 137); CPU over the limit = throttling
Make runtimes and worker pools aware of the limits
pitfalls: Setting a memory limit without telling the JVM, Node or worker pool, so the app is repeatedly OOM-killed.

quiz.q: A container exceeds its --cpus 1 limit under load. What happens?
options: It is throttled and runs slower
quiz.explain: CPU limits are enforced by throttling; only memory overuse leads to kills.

quiz.q: A container keeps exiting with code 137 and OOMKilled=true. What does that indicate?
options: It exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it
quiz.explain: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL); OOMKilled confirms the memory limit was hit.

concepts.name: BuildKit features
concepts.summary: Use BuildKit's cache mounts, secret and SSH mounts, heredocs and remote cache to make builds faster and safer.
concepts.why: These features cut CI build times dramatically and are the right way to use secrets during builds.
concepts.body:
**BuildKit** is Docker's build engine (the default since Engine 23; `docker build` is an alias for `docker buildx build`). Beyond parallel stages and skipping unused ones, it adds Dockerfile features. Start the file with `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` to get the latest stable syntax.

**Cache mounts** persist a directory across builds without putting it in the image:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Even when the layer's cache is invalidated, pip, npm, Go or apt find their download caches warm, so reinstalls take seconds.

**Secret mounts** expose a secret file to a single `RUN` without writing it into any layer or the build history:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci
```

and build with `docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc .`.

**SSH mounts** (`RUN --mount=type=ssh git clone git@github.com:acme/private.git` with `docker build --ssh default .`) forward your SSH agent for private dependencies, with no keys copied.

**Bind mounts** (`--mount=type=bind,source=.,target=/src`) read files from the context without a `COPY` layer, useful when only build output is needed.

**Heredocs** let you write multi-line scripts inline: `RUN <<EOF` ... `EOF`.

**Remote cache**: CI runners start with empty caches. `--cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/api:buildcache,mode=max` exports every layer's cache, and `--cache-from` with the same ref imports it on the next run (`type=gha` exists for GitHub Actions). Cache export to registries needs a builder using the docker-container driver or the containerd image store.

`docker buildx du` and `docker buildx prune` manage the builder's cache.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt,sharing=locked \
    rm -f /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/docker-clean && \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    --mount=type=bind,source=requirements.txt,target=requirements.txt \
    --mount=type=secret,id=pipconf,target=/etc/pip.conf \
    pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "main.py"]

# docker build --secret id=pipconf,src=$HOME/.config/pip/pip.conf \
#   --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/app:cache \
#   --cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/app:cache,mode=max -t app .
takeaways: RUN --mount=type=cache keeps package caches warm across builds
Secret and SSH mounts give a single step access without leaking into layers
Export/import cache to a registry so CI builds aren't cold
Begin Dockerfiles with # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
pitfalls: Expecting a cache mount's contents to be in the final image — they're only available during that RUN.

quiz.q: How does a BuildKit secret mount differ from COPY-ing a token file?
options: The secret is available only during that RUN and is never stored in a layer
It works only with Docker Hub
quiz.explain: Secret mounts are ephemeral, so the image and history never contain the secret.

quiz.q: Your CI builds always start cold. Which feature helps most?
options: --cache-to/--cache-from with a registry or gha cache
quiz.explain: Exporting and importing build cache lets fresh runners reuse previous layers.

concepts.name: Multi-platform builds
concepts.summary: Build one image tag for amd64 and arm64 with buildx, using emulation or faster cross-compilation.
concepts.why: Apple Silicon laptops, Graviton servers and Raspberry Pis all need arm64 images alongside amd64.
concepts.body:
An image built on an amd64 machine contains amd64 binaries and won't run natively on arm64 (and vice versa). A **multi-platform image** is one tag that points to an **image index** listing a separate image per platform; the client automatically pulls the one matching its architecture.

Build one with buildx:

```bash
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 --push .
```

The classic image store can't hold multi-platform images locally, so you either `--push` straight to a registry or use the **containerd image store** (the default in recent Docker Desktop installs), which can load them. A builder with the docker-container driver (`docker buildx create --use`) also works.

There are two ways to produce foreign-architecture binaries:

- **Emulation** with QEMU: BuildKit runs arm64 `RUN` steps under emulation. Docker Desktop includes it; on Linux install it with `docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install all`. It's simple but can be 5 to 20 times slower for compile-heavy steps.
- **Cross-compilation**: run the build stage on the builder's native platform and tell the compiler the target. BuildKit provides `BUILDPLATFORM`, `TARGETPLATFORM`, `TARGETOS` and `TARGETARCH` as automatic build args:

```dockerfile
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.25 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
RUN GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /app .
```

Go, Rust and Zig cross-compile easily, and Node or Python apps without native modules don't need compiling at all.

A third option is native builder nodes per architecture (`docker buildx create --append`) or arm64 CI runners. Check the result with `docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>`.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.25 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]

# docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
#   -t ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 --push .
# docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
#   Platform: linux/amd64 ... Platform: linux/arm64
takeaways: One tag, one image index, one image per platform
--platform a,b with --push (or the containerd image store to load locally)
Emulation is easy but slow; cross-compile with FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM
TARGETOS/TARGETARCH are provided automatically
pitfalls: Running every compile step under QEMU emulation and accepting 30-minute builds that cross-compilation would cut to minutes.

quiz.q: What does FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM achieve in a cross-compiling stage?
options: Forces the final image to the build machine's architecture
Runs the build stage natively on the builder, avoiding emulation
quiz.explain: The compiler runs natively and targets TARGETOS/TARGETARCH, so no QEMU is needed for that stage.

quiz.q: A user on an arm64 laptop runs docker pull of a multi-platform tag. What do they get?
options: The arm64 image, chosen from the index
quiz.explain: The client selects the matching platform entry from the image index.

concepts.name: Debugging containers
concepts.summary: Diagnose containers that crash, can't connect or have no shell, using logs, inspect, events, exit codes and debug sidecars.
concepts.why: Containers fail in container-specific ways, and minimal images strip out the usual tools.
concepts.body:
Work from the outside in.

**Why did it stop?** `docker ps -a` shows the exit code, and `docker logs` shows the last output. Common codes: `0` the process just finished (often a command that was meant to stay in the foreground); `1` an app error; `126` command not executable; `127` command not found (wrong `CMD`, or a script with Windows line endings or a missing interpreter); `137` SIGKILL (OOM or stop timeout); `143` SIGTERM. `docker inspect` gives `State`, `Config.Cmd`, `Mounts` and the effective `Env`.

**What is Docker doing?** `docker events` streams creates, starts, dies, OOM kills and health status changes.

**A container that crashes on start** can't be `exec`ed. Start the same image with a shell instead of its command: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myimage`, then run the real command by hand and watch it fail.

**Images without a shell** (distroless, scratch): attach a tools container to the target's namespaces. `docker run --rm -it --network container:api --pid container:api nicolaka/netshoot` shares its network and process view, so `curl localhost:8000`, `ss -lntp` and `ps` work against the target. Recent Docker Desktop versions offer `docker debug api`, which does this with a toolbox shell.

**Files**: `docker cp api:/app/log.txt .` copies out; `docker diff api` lists what changed in the writable layer.

**Network checklist** for "can't connect": same user-defined network? Using the service name, not `localhost`? Listening on `0.0.0.0`? Port published if the caller is outside Docker? `docker network inspect` and `nslookup` from a netshoot container answer each one.

**Build failures**: rerun with `--progress=plain --no-cache`, or build up to the failing stage with `--target` and run it interactively.
concepts.code:
docker ps -a --filter name=api --format '{{.Status}}'   # Exited (127) 3s ago
docker logs --tail 50 api
docker inspect api --format '{{json .Config.Cmd}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}'
docker events --filter container=api --since 10m

# Crash on start: get a shell in the same image instead
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh acme/api:1.4.2

# No shell in the image: borrow its network + PID namespaces
docker run --rm -it --network container:api --pid container:api \
  nicolaka/netshoot
#   ss -lntp ; curl -v localhost:8000/healthz ; ps aux

docker diff api            # A /tmp/x  C /etc  D /app/old.conf
docker cp api:/app/logs/error.log ./error.log
takeaways: Exit codes: 127 command not found, 137 SIGKILL/OOM, 143 SIGTERM
--entrypoint sh opens a shell in an image whose container crashes
--network/--pid container:<name> attaches a tools container to a shell-less one
docker events, inspect, diff and cp round out the toolkit
pitfalls: Trying to docker exec into a container that has already exited — start a fresh one with --entrypoint sh instead.

quiz.q: A container exits immediately with code 127. What is the most likely cause?
options: The command in CMD/ENTRYPOINT wasn't found in the image
The port is already in use
quiz.explain: 127 is the shell's 'command not found' code.

quiz.q: How can you run curl against a distroless container's localhost without changing its image?
options: Run a tools container with --network container:api
quiz.explain: Sharing the network namespace makes the target's localhost the tools container's localhost.

concepts.name: Compose for real projects
concepts.summary: Use override files, profiles, health-gated dependencies, interpolation and compose watch to run dev and CI from one setup.
concepts.why: Most teams' local environment and integration tests run on Compose; these features keep it maintainable.
concepts.body:
Once a project grows, a single flat `compose.yaml` starts to strain. Compose has tools for that.

**Override files.** `docker compose up` automatically merges `compose.override.yaml` on top of `compose.yaml`. Put production-like settings in the base and dev conveniences (bind mounts, debug ports) in the override. For other environments, pass files explicitly: `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml up`. Later files override or extend earlier ones.

**Profiles.** Mark optional services with `profiles: [tools]`; they start only with `--profile tools`. Good for admin UIs, seeders and load generators.

**Startup ordering.** `depends_on` conditions: `service_started`, `service_healthy` (requires a healthcheck) and `service_completed_successfully`, which is ideal for one-shot migration jobs that must finish before the app starts.

**Interpolation.** `${VAR}`, `${VAR:-default}` and `${VAR:?error message}` (fail if unset) come from the shell or the project's `.env`. Check the final, merged result with `docker compose config`; it's the best debugging tool for Compose files.

**Watch mode.** A `develop.watch` section plus `docker compose watch` syncs changed source files into running containers (`action: sync`), restarts on config changes (`sync+restart`) or rebuilds when dependencies change (`rebuild`). It replaces fragile bind mounts on Docker Desktop.

**Reuse.** `include:` pulls in other Compose files, such as a shared infrastructure stack, and YAML anchors or `extends` remove repetition.

**CI.** `docker compose up -d --wait` blocks until services are healthy, and `docker compose run --rm tests` runs one-off containers on the project network.
concepts.code:
services:
  migrate:
    build: .
    command: ["alembic", "upgrade", "head"]
    depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:${API_PORT:-8000}:8000"]
    environment:
      SECRET_KEY: ${SECRET_KEY:?set SECRET_KEY in .env}
    depends_on:
      migrate: { condition: service_completed_successfully }
    develop:
      watch:
        - { action: sync, path: ./src, target: /app/src }
        - { action: rebuild, path: requirements.txt }
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev }
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"], interval: 5s }
  adminer:
    image: adminer
    profiles: [tools]
# docker compose config ; docker compose watch ; docker compose --profile tools up -d
takeaways: compose.override.yaml is merged automatically; -f stacks files explicitly
profiles make services optional; service_completed_successfully gates on jobs
docker compose config shows the fully merged, interpolated file
compose watch syncs or rebuilds on file changes
pitfalls: Debugging a confusing setup without running docker compose config to see what Compose actually resolved.

quiz.q: Which depends_on condition fits a database migration job that must finish before the API starts?
quiz.explain: It waits for the dependency to run to completion with exit code 0.

quiz.q: You run docker compose up in a folder with compose.yaml and compose.override.yaml. What is used?
options: Both, with the override merged on top
quiz.explain: Compose loads the override file automatically when no -f is given.

concepts.name: Namespaces and cgroups
concepts.summary: Containers are built from Linux namespaces (what a process can see) and cgroups (what it can use).
