concepts.why: Knowing the kernel primitives demystifies isolation, limits and many container bugs.
concepts.body:
There is no "container" object in the Linux kernel. A container is an ordinary process set up with two families of kernel features.

**Namespaces** control what a process can **see**. Each kind gives the process its own view of one global resource:

- `pid`: its own process tree; the app is PID 1 and can't see host processes.
- `net`: its own interfaces, IPs, routing table and ports (a veth pair connects it to the bridge).
- `mnt`: its own mount table, with the image's root filesystem as `/`.
- `uts`: its own hostname. `ipc`: its own shared memory and semaphores.
- `user`: maps UIDs inside to different UIDs outside (used by rootless mode and userns-remap).
- `cgroup` and `time`: virtualized views of the cgroup tree and of some clocks.

Docker's flags map straight onto these: `--network host` and `--pid host` mean *don't* create that namespace, and `--network container:x` *joins* another container's namespace.

**Control groups (cgroups)** control what a process can **use**: memory, CPU time, I/O bandwidth and number of PIDs, with accounting for each. Modern hosts use **cgroup v2**, a single unified hierarchy under `/sys/fs/cgroup`. With the systemd cgroup driver, a container lives in a scope like `system.slice/docker-<id>.scope`, where files such as `memory.max`, `cpu.max` and `pids.max` hold the limits you set with `--memory`, `--cpus` and `--pids-limit`.

Since a container is just a process, the host sees it: `ps` on the host lists it with a host PID, and `nsenter` can enter its namespaces. Together with capabilities, seccomp and LSMs (AppArmor/SELinux), these features make up container isolation, all sharing one kernel.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name web --memory 256m --cpus 0.5 nginx:1.27
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web)
ps -o pid,user,cmd -p "$PID"            # visible from the host
sudo ls -l /proc/$PID/ns                # net -> net:[4026532301] ...
sudo lsns -p "$PID"

# Enter just its network namespace with host tools
sudo nsenter -t "$PID" -n ip addr

# Its cgroup v2 limits (systemd driver)
CG=$(awk -F: '{print $3}' /proc/$PID/cgroup)
cat /sys/fs/cgroup$CG/memory.max        # 268435456
cat /sys/fs/cgroup$CG/cpu.max           # 50000 100000
takeaways: Namespaces limit what a process sees: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time
cgroups limit and account what it uses: memory, CPU, I/O, PIDs
--network host / container:x skip or share a namespace
A container is a host process; nsenter and /proc reveal it
pitfalls: Treating namespace isolation as a security boundary equal to a VM — all containers share one kernel.

quiz.q: Which mechanism enforces --memory 256m?
quiz.explain: cgroups limit resource usage; namespaces only change visibility.

quiz.q: What does docker run --pid host do?
options: Gives the container its own PID 1
Hides the host's processes more strongly
Skips creating a PID namespace, so the container sees all host processes
quiz.explain: Host mode means the container shares the host's namespace instead of getting a new one.

concepts.name: Union filesystems and overlayfs
concepts.summary: How overlayfs stacks read-only image layers under a writable container layer, with copy-up and whiteouts.
concepts.why: It explains layer sharing, slow first writes to big files and why data belongs in volumes.
concepts.body:
A container's root filesystem is a **union mount**: several directories stacked so they appear as one. On Linux, Docker uses the kernel's **overlayfs**, either through the `overlay2` storage driver or, with the containerd image store, containerd's overlayfs snapshotter. `docker info` shows which.

An overlay mount has:

- **lowerdir**: one or more read-only directories, the image layers, stacked top to bottom.
- **upperdir**: the container's writable layer.
- **workdir**: scratch space the kernel needs for atomic operations.
- **merged**: the unified view that becomes the container's `/`.

Reads fall through the stack: the topmost layer that has a file wins. Because lower layers are read-only and identified by content, a hundred containers from the same image share one copy on disk and in the page cache.

Writes follow **copy-on-write**:

- Modifying a file from a lower layer first triggers a **copy-up**: the *whole* file is copied into upperdir, then modified. The first write to a 2 GB file copies 2 GB. That's one reason databases and other write-heavy data belong on volumes, which bypass the overlay entirely.
- Deleting a lower file creates a **whiteout** in upperdir (a 0/0 character device) that hides it; the data still exists below.
- Replacing a directory uses an **opaque** marker so lower contents are hidden.

Image layers work the same way at build time: each layer tarball stores additions plus whiteout entries (`.wh.<name>` in the tar format). That's why deleting files in a later Dockerfile step never shrinks an image.

Inspect a container's overlay with `docker inspect -f '{{json .GraphDriver.Data}}'` (overlay2 driver) or `mount | grep overlay`.
concepts.code:
docker info --format '{{.Driver}}'          # overlay2 (or overlayfs via containerd)
docker run -d --name t alpine sleep 1d
docker inspect t --format '{{json .GraphDriver.Data}}' | tr ',' '\n'
# "LowerDir":"/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>-init/diff:/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<layer>/diff"
# "MergedDir":".../merged"  "UpperDir":".../diff"  "WorkDir":".../work"

docker exec t sh -c 'echo x >> /etc/hosts.allow; rm /etc/motd'
UPPER=$(docker inspect t --format '{{.GraphDriver.Data.UpperDir}}')
sudo ls -l "$UPPER/etc"
# -rw-r--r-- ... hosts.allow    <- copied up, then modified
# c--------- 0, 0 ... motd       <- whiteout hiding the lower file
docker diff t                    # C /etc  A /etc/hosts.allow  D /etc/motd
takeaways: lowerdir = read-only image layers, upperdir = container layer, merged = /
First write to a lower file copies the whole file up
Deletes are whiteouts; the data stays in the lower layer
Write-heavy data belongs on volumes, outside the overlay
pitfalls: Storing a large, frequently written file (like a SQLite DB) in the image and paying copy-up plus overlay overhead in every container.

quiz.q: A container appends one line to a 1 GB log file that came from the image. What does overlayfs do?
options: Writes only the new line to the upper layer
Copies the entire 1 GB file to the upper layer, then appends
Modifies the image layer in place
Fails because image layers are read-only
quiz.explain: Copy-up operates on whole files on first write.

quiz.q: How does overlayfs represent a file deleted in the container but present in the image?
options: A whiteout entry in the upper layer hides it
The file is removed from the lower layer
It isn't possible to delete it
quiz.explain: Lower layers are never modified; a whiteout masks the file in the merged view.

concepts.name: OCI image and runtime specs
concepts.summary: Images are OCI artifacts: content-addressed manifests, configs and layer blobs; runtimes execute an OCI bundle.
concepts.why: The open specs are why images built by Docker run on Kubernetes, Podman and any registry.
concepts.body:
The **Open Container Initiative** (OCI) defines three specifications that make containers portable between tools.

The **image spec** describes an image as content-addressed blobs, each referenced by a **descriptor** (media type, `sha256` digest, size):

- An **image index** lists manifests per platform (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`), plus, in images built by buildx, attestation manifests such as SBOMs and provenance.
- An **image manifest** points to one **config** blob and an ordered list of **layer** blobs.
- The **config** JSON holds the runtime defaults (`Entrypoint`, `Cmd`, `Env`, `User`, `WorkingDir`), the history, and the `rootfs.diff_ids`: digests of the *uncompressed* layers.
- **Layers** are tar archives of filesystem changes (with whiteouts), usually gzip- or zstd-compressed; their digest in the manifest is of the compressed bytes.

The image's digest is the hash of its manifest (or index). Since that manifest names every blob by hash, one digest pins every byte. Docker's own v2 manifest format is a near twin and both are accepted everywhere.

The **distribution spec** is the registry HTTP API: `GET /v2/<name>/manifests/<reference>` and `GET /v2/<name>/blobs/<digest>`, with uploads in chunks. Registries now also store non-image artifacts such as Helm charts, signatures and SBOMs, linked through the `subject` field (the referrers API).

The **runtime spec** defines a **bundle**: a root filesystem directory plus `config.json` describing the process, mounts, namespaces, cgroups, capabilities and seccomp profile, and the lifecycle operations (create, start, kill, delete). runc is the reference implementation; the engine translates image config plus `docker run` flags into that `config.json`.
concepts.code:
# Index -> per-platform manifests
docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw nginx:1.27 | head -20
# {"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
#  "manifests":[{"digest":"sha256:...","platform":{"architecture":"amd64","os":"linux"}}, ...]}

# One manifest: config + layers (crane is a small registry CLI)
crane manifest --platform linux/arm64 nginx:1.27
# {"config":{"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.image.config.v1+json","digest":"sha256:..."},
#  "layers":[{"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar+gzip","digest":"sha256:...","size":29136913}, ...]}

crane config nginx:1.27 | jq '.config.Cmd, .rootfs.diff_ids[0]'

# Generate a runtime-spec config.json
mkdir bundle && cd bundle && runc spec && jq '.process.args, .linux.namespaces' config.json
takeaways: Index -> manifest -> config + layers, all addressed by sha256 digest
The image digest is the manifest's hash, pinning every byte
Distribution spec = registry HTTP API; registries also store artifacts
Runtime spec = rootfs + config.json, executed by runc
pitfalls: Comparing layer digests from the manifest with config diff_ids — one is of compressed bytes, the other uncompressed, so they differ.

quiz.q: What is a multi-platform image tag at the registry level?
options: One manifest containing every architecture's layers
An image index pointing to one manifest per platform
A compressed tar of all images
quiz.explain: The index lists per-platform manifests; clients pick the matching one.

quiz.q: Why does pinning an image by digest guarantee identical contents?
options: The digest is a hash of the manifest, which names every blob by hash
quiz.explain: Content addressing chains hashes from manifest to config and layers.

concepts.name: Engine architecture: dockerd, containerd, runc
concepts.summary: Follow docker run through the CLI, dockerd, containerd, the shim and runc, and see why each layer exists.
concepts.why: Architecture knowledge explains daemon restarts, alternative runtimes and Kubernetes' relationship to Docker.
concepts.body:
`docker run` passes through several components, each with a narrow job.

- **docker CLI**: a client that sends REST calls to the daemon's API, by default over `/var/run/docker.sock` (or a remote host through `DOCKER_HOST` or contexts).
- **dockerd**: the Docker Engine. It owns Docker's user-facing features: the API, image builds (via BuildKit), networks, volumes, Compose support and logging drivers.
- **containerd**: a container supervisor (a graduated CNCF project) that manages images, snapshots (filesystem layers) and container lifecycles behind a gRPC API. Kubernetes talks to containerd directly through CRI, which is why Kubernetes removed the Docker-specific shim and why "Kubernetes dropped Docker" changed little for images.
- **containerd-shim-runc-v2**: one small shim per container. It becomes the container's parent, holds its stdio and exit status, and lets dockerd and containerd restart without killing containers (enable `live-restore` in `daemon.json` for the full effect).
- **runc**: the OCI runtime. It reads the bundle's `config.json`, creates namespaces and cgroups, applies capabilities, seccomp and mounts, `exec`s the container process, then **exits**. It is not a long-running daemon.

Because the runtime is pluggable, you can swap it per container: `--runtime runsc` (gVisor, a user-space kernel for strong isolation), Kata Containers (lightweight VMs) or alternative OCI runtimes such as crun or youki. `docker info` shows registered runtimes and the default.

Tools exist at each level: `ctr` and `nerdctl` talk to containerd directly, and `runc list` shows runc's view. Docker namespaces its containers in containerd as `moby`, so `sudo ctr -n moby containers ls` lists them.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name demo nginx:1.27
ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -C containerd-shim-runc-v2,nginx
#   PID  PPID CMD
#  4120     1 /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v2 -namespace moby -id 5c1e...
#  4141  4120 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;

sudo ctr -n moby containers ls          # same container, seen by containerd
docker info --format '{{.DefaultRuntime}} {{json .Runtimes}}'

# /etc/docker/daemon.json: keep containers running across daemon restarts
#   { "live-restore": true }
sudo systemctl restart docker && docker ps   # demo is still up

docker run --rm --runtime runsc alpine uname -a   # if gVisor is installed
takeaways: CLI -> dockerd (API, builds, networks) -> containerd -> shim -> runc
runc sets up the container and exits; the shim stays as its parent
Shims plus live-restore keep containers alive across daemon restarts
Runtimes are pluggable: gVisor, Kata, crun via --runtime
pitfalls: Exposing the Docker API socket or TCP port without TLS — it grants root on the host.

quiz.q: Which component remains the parent process of a running container after it starts?
quiz.explain: runc exits after creating the container; the shim supervises it.

quiz.q: Kubernetes removed dockershim. Why do images built with Docker still run on it?
options: They are OCI images, and containerd/CRI-O run OCI images
Docker is still embedded in kubelet
They don't; images must be rebuilt
quiz.explain: Images follow the OCI spec, so any compliant runtime can run them.

concepts.name: Rootless mode, capabilities and seccomp
concepts.summary: Reduce container privileges with dropped capabilities, seccomp, no-new-privileges, user namespaces and rootless Docker.
concepts.why: Defence in depth turns a container compromise into a contained incident instead of a host takeover.
concepts.body:
Root in a container is the host's UID 0 (unless user namespaces are used), restricted by several layers. Knowing them lets you tighten each.

**Capabilities** split root's power into units. Docker grants a reduced default set (including `CHOWN`, `DAC_OVERRIDE`, `SETUID`, `SETGID`, `NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `NET_RAW`, `KILL`) and withholds dangerous ones like `SYS_ADMIN`, `SYS_MODULE` and `NET_ADMIN`. Best practice: `--cap-drop ALL`, then `--cap-add` only what's needed.

**seccomp** filters system calls. Docker's default profile blocks dozens of risky syscalls (kernel module loading, `reboot`, `kexec_load`, `mount` without the right capability...) while allowing what normal apps use. Custom profiles go in with `--security-opt seccomp=profile.json`. Never use `seccomp=unconfined` casually.

**`--security-opt no-new-privileges`** stops setuid binaries and file capabilities from granting more privilege than the process started with.

**LSMs**: AppArmor (`docker-default` profile) or SELinux labels add mandatory access control on files and mounts.

**`--privileged`** turns nearly all of this off: all capabilities, all devices, no seccomp. It is effectively host root, so avoid it outside of special cases such as Docker-in-Docker or hardware access.

**User namespaces** remap container root to an unprivileged host UID. `userns-remap` in `daemon.json` does this for all containers. **Rootless mode** goes further: the daemon itself runs as a normal user (`dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install`), using subordinate UID ranges from `/etc/subuid` and RootlessKit for networking. A full escape then yields only that user's rights. Trade-offs: binding ports below 1024 needs a sysctl change, and some networking and storage features are limited.

Combine these with a non-root `USER` and a read-only root filesystem for strong defaults.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name api \
  --user 10001:10001 \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
  --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -p 80:80 acme/api:1.4.2

docker inspect api --format '{{.HostConfig.CapDrop}} {{.HostConfig.SecurityOpt}}'
docker run --rm alpine grep Cap /proc/self/status     # default capability bitmasks

# Rootless Docker for the current user
dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install
export DOCKER_HOST=unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock
docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}'   # [name=seccomp,... name=rootless ...]
takeaways: Drop all capabilities and add back only what's needed
The default seccomp profile blocks risky syscalls; don't run unconfined
--privileged disables almost all isolation
userns-remap or rootless mode map container root to an unprivileged host user
pitfalls: Reaching for --privileged to fix a permission error instead of adding the single capability or device actually required.

quiz.q: Which flag most effectively removes root powers a web app doesn't need?
quiz.explain: Dropping every capability then adding back only what's needed minimises privilege.

quiz.q: In rootless mode, what does root inside a container correspond to on the host?
options: The unprivileged user running the rootless daemon (via user namespaces)
quiz.explain: Rootless Docker maps container UIDs into that user's subordinate UID range.
